content: Paget's disease of the breast is characterized by eczematous changes in the skin of the nipple, often associated with an underlying breast malignancy. The hallmark features include erythema and eczematous alterations of the nipple, first described by Velpeau in 1856. The epidermotropic theory, which suggests that carcinoma cells from the ducts migrate to the nipple, was supported by Muir and Inglis in 1939 and 1946, respectively. This condition accounts for 1–4% of all female breast carcinoma cases and is invariably linked to an underlying malignancy, either overt or occult. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates 800,000 to 1 million new cases of breast cancer annually, with over 90% of Paget's disease cases involving an underlying breast carcinoma. Most of these are invasive, although 40–45% are associated with ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS). Paget's disease is more common in postmenopausal women, typically after the sixth decade of life, but it has also been reported in adolescents and elderly patients. Females are more frequently affected than males. Male breast cancer constitutes less than 1% of all breast cancers, and Paget's disease represents 1–3% of all breast malignancies. Mammary Paget's disease is almost always associated with underlying breast cancer in 92–100% of cases, with approximately 50% of patients presenting with a palpable breast mass. Histopathologically, Paget cells are malignant glandular epithelial cells found in the epidermis, often organized in nest-like patterns or gland-like structures, predominantly in the basal layer. Risk factors for developing Paget's disease include female sex, increasing age, African or Ashkenazi Jewish descent, personal or family history of breast cancer, and environmental exposures such as radiation, high temperatures, and electromagnetic fields. Genetic mutations, including BRCA1, BRCA2, RAD51B, PALB2, CYP17, CHEK2, BRIP1, and RAD51C, are implicated, with BRIP1 and RAD51C not observed in male patients. Endocrine-related conditions with hyperestrogenism, such as obesity, exogenous estrogen use, and testicular dystrophic lesions in males, are also associated. Symptoms of Paget's disease include itching, redness, thickened skin, and ulceration of the nipple, which may spread to the areola and surrounding skin. The lesion is sharply demarcated from adjacent normal skin and may present as a round, ovoid, or polycyclic eczema-like plaque with pink or red discoloration. Physical examination often reveals an eczematous appearance of the nipple with yellowish or bloody discharge. Diagnosis may be delayed or misdiagnosed due to similarities with other skin lesions. Immunohistochemical staining for cytokeratin, epithelial membrane antigen (EMA), and c-erbB-2 oncoprotein aids in differential diagnosis. Toker cells, found in the epidermis near lactiferous duct openings, are morphologically and immunohistochemically similar to Paget cells but can be distinguished using markers like Ki-67 and Her-2/c-erbB-2. Atypical Toker cells can be differentiated from Paget cells using CD138 and p53. Paget's disease must be distinguished from atopic dermatitis, eczema, psoriasis, malignant melanoma, Bowen's disease, basal cell carcinoma, benign intraductal papilloma, nevoid hyperkeratosis of the nipple and areola (NHNA), squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts (SMOLD)/Zuska's disease, and pagetoid dyskeratosis. The prognosis of Paget's disease is primarily determined by the underlying tumor. Poor prognosis is associated with palpable breast tumors, enlarged lymph nodes, and younger age (<60 years). Prognosis is worse in males than females, with five-year survival rates of 20–30% in males compared to 30–40% in females. This disparity is hypothesized to result from the smaller size of mammary glands in males. A full-thickness biopsy of the nipple and areola is crucial for diagnosis, with findings of Paget cells arranged in solid groups being diagnostic. Breast ultrasonography and MRI are valuable for detecting associated breast cancer, especially in cases with negative mammography. MRI is also useful for preoperative evaluation and treatment planning. Mammography, while commonly used, has limited reliability in detecting underlying DCIS in Paget's disease. Cytological diagnosis using touch or scrape smears is recommended to prevent diagnostic delays, particularly in patients reluctant to undergo invasive procedures. Treatment typically involves surgery, with mastectomy being the mainstay. Patients without a palpable lump are treated with nipple and areola removal followed by whole-breast radiation therapy. Those with associated DCIS or invasive breast cancer require complete resection of the underlying disease, including excision of the nipple-areola complex and radiation therapy to the remaining breast tissue. In cases with lymph node involvement, more extensive axillary lymph node surgery may be necessary, along with adjunctive radiation. Chemotherapy and radiotherapy are indicated as adjuvant or palliative treatments in patients with underlying ductal carcinoma or invasive breast cancer.
